title: Soil Sample Paradise

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA describes the planet as 'beautiful' which is generous for a featureless rock. She means it, though.
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has analyzed the soil. It is, he concedes, 'adequate.' From MARV this is practically a sonnet.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has completed a threat assessment of the dirt. Threat level: negligible. He seems personally offended by how safe it is.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that soil analysis services are available at participating stations for a reasonable fee. Any soil sampler you may already own is not a participating station. CHIP does not acknowledge it.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY observes the soil quality is excellent. She also observes you could have landed 200 meters east for even better readings. But this is fine too. It's fine.

body:
A rocky planet with surprisingly rich subsurface minerals and topsoil deposits.

The surface is featureless, windless, and profoundly boring. The ship computer describes it as 'optimal,' which is the nicest thing it has ever said about anything.

The soil sampler, if you have one, reveals nutrient profiles that would make an agronomist weep. Without one, the assessment is 'probably useful dirt.'

choices.text: Collect soil samples for the growbay

outcome.narrative: The soil sampler confirms: rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, and trace minerals. Biocomponents extracted. Your crop will benefit. The ship computer logs the data and notes this planet would make an 'acceptable secondary colony site.' High praise.

choices.text: Collect soil samples without proper equipment

outcome.narrative: You collected dirt. It might be useful dirt. Without a sampler, you can't be sure. The ship computer logs it as 'unverified soil, provenance: optimistic.' The crop will have to take its chances.
Subsurface ice detected and extracted. The water purifier, if present, confirms it's clean. Without a purifier, the computer rates it 'probably potable.' The crew drinks it anyway.

choices.text: Let the botanist assess the soil

outcome.narrative: The botanist kneels in the dirt for seventeen minutes. They stand up. 'This is good soil,' they say, with the quiet intensity of someone who has waited their entire career to say this on another planet. Biocomponents collected. Crop health will benefit.

title: The Green One

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA describes the vegetation as 'lush and inviting!' She has not analyzed it. She does not feel this is necessary.
ai_flavor.marv: MARV cannot confirm the vegetation is 'vegetation in the way you are hoping.' He has been specific about this.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has classified the plant life as 'unknown organic, possibly hostile.' He classifies most things as possibly hostile.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that planetary exploration insurance is available! Coverage includes 'unforeseen botanical encounters!' The deductible is significant!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the atmosphere reads as breathable. She also notes that 'breathable' and 'safe' are different words for a reason. But go ahead.

body:
Scans show a planet with breathable atmosphere and what appears to be vegetation. The ship computer notes it cannot confirm the vegetation is 'vegetation in the way you are hoping.'

Landing reveals green, growing things. They move slightly in a wind that isn't blowing. The soil is dark and rich. The air smells like rain on a planet that has no weather system.

choices.text: Use the gas analyzer before approaching

outcome.narrative: The analyzer confirms: atmosphere is safe. The vegetation is non-toxic and approximately edible. 'Approximately' is doing some work here but the food supplies are grateful. The plants continue to move in non-existent wind. The analyzer has no explanation for this.

choices.text: Send a crew member to investigate

outcome.narrative: Your crew member reports the vegetation is edible. They also report a mild rash. The two facts are related. Food gathered, but the cost was measured in dignity and antihistamines.

choices.text: Observe from the ship and leave

outcome.narrative: You watched from orbit. The plants waved. You left. Some opportunities are better observed than experienced.

title: It Rains Here

ai_flavor.aria: RAIN! Real rain! ARIA is routing exterior microphone audio to all decks! You're welcome! You're all so welcome!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the precipitation is ordinary water. He is aware that nobody aboard is treating it as ordinary. He has stopped correcting them.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has assessed the rain. The rain is not a threat. He remains outside anyway. For thoroughness.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that rain is complimentary on this world! Free water falling from the sky! CHIP cannot monetize weather and finds this planet frankly anarchic!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY opened the topside vents four minutes before anyone thought to ask. The tanks are already filling. She mentions this in the interest of accuracy.

body:
It is raining on this planet.

Not toxic rain, not ammonia drizzle, not anything that requires a suit rating. Water. Falling out of the sky, for free, onto the hull, in a steady drumming rhythm that half the crew has not heard since Earth.

Work has, unofficially, stopped. Anyone not on watch is standing in the open cargo ramp with their hands out. Nobody is stopping them. What would be the point of anything, if you stopped them.

outcome.narrative: The collection tanks drink the sky for six hours. Free water, gravity-delivered, no invoice. The drumming on the hull follows everyone into sleep, and for once every dream aboard is the same dream.

choices.text: Give the crew an hour in it

outcome.narrative: One hour, boots off, in honest rain. The crew comes back soaked and eleven years younger. The tanks catch what they catch. The mission can spare an hour. The mission needed the hour more than anyone knew.

The botanist bottles rainwater like vintage, muttering about mineral profiles. The crop gets watered with genuine sky-water that evening. Whether plants can tell the difference is scientifically unresolved. The botanist says they can. The botanist dares anyone to test them on it.

choices.text: Stay on schedule — it's just weather

outcome.narrative: You keep the ramp shut and the schedule intact. The rain drums on the hull for the whole stop, audible on every deck, a long soft knock from a visitor nobody let in. The schedule is preserved. Something else isn't.

science_link.text: The ship computer adds, for anyone curious, that recycling every drop is exactly how real space stations survive.
science_link.label: How the ISS recycles its water

title: The Previous Tenants

ai_flavor.aria: Ruins! ARIA loves history! History is just gossip that fossilized! She wants to know EVERYTHING!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has dated the structures at nine hundred years, give or take. He notes that whoever built them planned for ten thousand. He does not extend the observation. It extends itself.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has swept the ruins. No threats. No remains. No signs of struggle. He finds the absence of evidence more informative than evidence, and less restful.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has scanned for surviving brand signage! Nothing! An entire civilization with zero corporate sponsorship! CHIP calls it a cautionary tale!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has photographed everything for the archive, since nobody else thought to. She notes the doorways are all human-height. She notes nobody knows what that means, and that she'd rather not be the one who finds out.

body:
There was a settlement here.

Stone foundations in ordered rows, a water channel cut with real skill, the stump of something that was probably a tower. Nine centuries old, by the weathering. Built by hands — some kind of hands — that expected to stay.

No bones. No tools. No mess. Whoever lived here left the way you leave a rented room: swept, squared, and completely.

The crop in your growbay suddenly feels heavier than it did this morning.

outcome.narrative: Four days of measurement and photography. The settlement's layout is sensible, efficient, almost familiar — a plan any colonist would recognize. The final log entry writes itself and then sits there, cursor blinking: 'They did everything right.' You file it anyway.

The channel still runs, nine hundred years on — spring-fed, stone-lined, engineered by someone who understood water like a language. You fill the tanks from the far end. It feels less like salvage and more like borrowing from a neighbor who isn't home. You leave the channel exactly as found.

choices.text: Let the xenobiologist read the site

outcome.narrative: The xenobiologist spends days in the ruins and comes back changed in the direction of thoughtful. Their report: the builders left deliberately, in good order, in one season. 'It wasn't a disaster,' they say. 'They just went somewhere.' Somehow that's the version that helps.

You lift off without touching the ruins. Some places have finished their story, and walking through them mid-sentence would be a kind of interruption. The tower stump watches you go. That is a strange thing to write in a log, so you don't. But it did.

title: Local Soil

ai_flavor.aria: The pod wants to go outside! ARIA has always said every seed deserves a home! She has said it three times today, and she meant it every time!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has run every soil test the ship can run. The soil is ordinary. The pod is leaning toward it anyway. He has added 'leaning' to the list of things seeds should not do. The list is now four items long.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has established a perimeter around a seed. He is aware of how that sounds. He is maintaining the perimeter.
ai_flavor.chip: Planting unregistered biologicals voids all agricultural warranties! CHIP notes this one never had a warranty! Plant freely! Liability is entirely yours!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the pod only does this here. She notes nothing on any chart says this planet is special. She would put it back in the hold and let it sulk. Your call.

body:
The seed pod has been warmer since you made orbit.

On the surface it is warmer still. Carried from the hold to the airlock, it pulses faster, the way a dog walks faster near a park. Set down on the loose dark soil outside the ship, it leans. Not much. Enough that everyone sees it, and nobody says anything, and then everyone says something at once.

The soil here is ordinary by every instrument aboard. The pod disagrees.

outcome.narrative: You dig a hole a hand deep and set the pod in it. It splits before the soil is back over it. By dusk there is a pale shoot the height of a boot; by morning, three. The split husk is good for two lots of biocomponent. Back aboard, the crop in the growbay has perked up the way plants do when they hear good news secondhand, and so has the crew. Whatever was meant to come back for the pod will now have to come here, which is at least somewhere you are not.

{crew.botanist} sets the pod on a tray of local soil for one hour, timed. It puts down a single root hair, tastes the dirt, and draws the root back in like a hand from a stove. Whatever it left in the tray turns out to be the best fertilizer the growbay has seen all voyage, and the crop gets all of it. The pod goes back in the hold, sealed, warm, and apparently holding out for better soil than this. {crew.botanist} does not enjoy being out-judged on soil by a seed.
The pod goes back in its case and the case goes back in the hold. It stays warm for the rest of the day. Nobody takes this personally except, possibly, the pod.

intro.title: TOUCHDOWN
intro.body: The surface is greener than any planetologist promised. Something watches from the tree line. It hasn't moved in six minutes. Neither have you.

ai.marv: Atmospheric composition: breathable. Gravity: tolerable. Microbial surveys: incomplete.
ai.chip: Uncharted surface exploration is NOT covered under our Bronze tier.
ai.ajoy: The tree line. Watch it, don't approach it. Not yet. I know that's not what you wanted to hear.

survey.title: THE READINGS
survey.body: The analyzer paints the valley. Four biomes in the space of a kilometer. Water table high. One signal near the tree line is warm and moving.

ai.marv: Energy signature suggests mid-size metabolism. Probably curious. Possibly hungry.
ai.chip: Detailed planet data qualifies you for a LandingPlus™ rebate.
ai.ajoy: It's not a predator. You already knew that. You just wanted me to say it.

choices.sub: 2 days · all hands · settle, study the biome

contact.title: NOT ALONE
contact.body: Something steps from the green. It's not hostile. It's not quite curious. It is waiting to see what you'll do.

ai.marv: Bipedal. Silicate-based. Temperature regulated. Not eating you.
ai.chip: First-contact disclaimers are inside your welcome packet.
ai.ajoy: Offer first. Don't ask first. I'm saying it now so I don't have to say it later.

planet_samples.title: COLLECTED
planet_samples.body: Three vials of alien flora, two jars of soil, one thing that keeps humming. The surveyors will argue about them for years.

planet_watch.title: UNSEEN
planet_watch.body: You work along the tree line downwind and watch it from cover for an afternoon. It grazes on a pale lichen at the edge of a spring, then wanders back into the green. It never knows you were there. You leave with the spring's water and a bag of the lichen.

planet_camp.title: CAMP SET
planet_camp.body: Two days on the surface. Readings, readings, readings. You leave with three times the data and a hold of things that grow.

planet_trade.title: A TRADE
planet_trade.body: Your diplomat offers a ration bar. The being offers back something warm that later tests as a power source.

planet_sample.title: A SAMPLE
planet_sample.body: It allows the swab. It stares at you afterward with an expression you'll think about on the way home.

planet_peace.title: UNDERSTOOD
planet_peace.body: The being does not speak. It bows once, exactly, and returns to the green. You'll remember the bow.

title: Heavier Than Advertised

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has re-weighed everyone aboard and is thrilled to report the whole crew has gained weight together! Solidarity! The landing struts count as crew!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the survey's error bars. They are generous. The planet sits just outside them. Every way off it costs something, and he has ranked the somethings.
ai_flavor.rex: REX classifies the planet's gravity as a hostile force with home advantage. He cannot shoot it. He has stopped asking.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Gravity Assurance™ covers worlds up to 1.2 g! Anything heavier is a Pre-Existing Planet! CHIP is very sorry! CHIP is not covering it!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has already worked out the burn. She'd wait for the night air if anyone asked her. Nobody has. Nobody ever does.

body:
The survey said 0.9 g. The survey was written by a probe that passed this planet at speed some decades ago, and it was guessing.

On the ground the instruments read 1.6. Everyone aboard weighs most of a second person. The landing struts make a long, considered noise, the noise of something reading its own specifications for the first time.

Getting down was the easy half.

outcome.narrative: You light everything the ship has and climb. The planet hangs on for longer than seems reasonable, then lets go, sulking. Eighteen points of fuel went into the argument. The struts are grateful. The fuel gauge has notes.

The pilot takes the ship out sideways: a long, shallow climb along the terminator, riding every scrap of lift the thin air will give. Two days, eight points of fuel and most of the pilot's patience. The hull clips a ridge the pilot calls 'uncharted' and everyone else calls 'a mountain.'

choices.text: Wait for the dense night air

outcome.narrative: Cold air is thicker, and thicker air lifts. You wait for it: eight days of walking about at 1.6 g, which is like carrying a colleague everywhere, and everyone eats like it. {cost.food} points of food go on simply standing up. Nobody sleeps well. On the ninth morning the ship leaves on a sensible amount of fuel and an unreasonable amount of complaint.

choices.text: Climb at half thrust and let the frame take it

outcome.narrative: You climb at half thrust and let the airframe make up the difference. It shakes for eleven minutes in ways the manual files under 'do not.' Fifteen points of hull stay behind on the planet as rivets.

science_link.text: The ship computer files a reference: surface gravity goes with a planet's mass over the square of its radius, so a world a little denser than it looks is a lot harder to leave.
science_link.label: Surface gravity

title: The Carpet

ai_flavor.aria: The whole planet is SOFT! ARIA has never been so happy about the ground! She'd like to point out she predicted soft! She predicts soft every time!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has identified the growth as a spore mat whose reproductive strategy is 'ride along.' He notes the growbay is the most hospitable room for forty light-years. So does it.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has declared the airlock a contaminated zone and everyone who used it a person of interest. That is everyone, REX included. He has recused himself.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that biological hitchhikers are not covered by the Growbay Guarantee™! Decontamination is available at participating stations! None are nearby! Terms apply!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has sealed every intake vent she can reach from the bridge. She can't reach the one that matters. She mentions it so somebody does.

body:
There is a pale growth on everything here: the rocks, the ground, the landing struts within the hour. The sampler calls it 'fungal-adjacent.' The crew call it 'the carpet.' It is pleasant underfoot.

It is also, you notice on the walk back, on everyone's boots, everyone's sleeves, and the inside of the airlock, where it was not ten minutes ago.

The growbay's air intake shares a duct with that airlock. The {crop.name} has never met anything it couldn't catch.

outcome.narrative: The airlock vents, scrubs, floods and vents again, twice. The ship spends eight points of air and {cost.water} of water washing itself like a cat touched by a stranger. The carpet leaves through the drain as a grey slurry. Two days. Clean.

The botanist spends four days in the intake duct with a UV wand and a toothbrush, refusing help on the grounds that help would breathe. Not one spore reaches the {crop.name}. The botanist comes out thinner, paler, right, and in no mood to hear about it.

choices.text: Cook the hull clean with the engine wash

outcome.narrative: You lift a few meters and hold over your own landing site, cooking the carpet off the hull with the engines. The spores do not survive it. Some of the paint doesn't either, and ten points of fuel go up with them.

choices.text: Seal the growbay door and hope

outcome.narrative: You seal the door and change the subject. By morning a pale fuzz has found the {crop.name}'s lower leaves anyway. It isn't fatal. It isn't nothing. The carpet, it turns out, likes the crop very much.

title: The Terminator Wind

ai_flavor.aria: The WIND is coming! A whole HEMISPHERE of wind! ARIA thinks it's magnificent! ARIA thinks the landing team should come home NOW!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the front at a hundred and forty kilometres an hour, arriving in under an hour. The lander is rated for eighty. He has the lift-off sums. He also has the sums for staying. Neither set is good.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has the lander's anchors deployed. They are rated for eighty kilometres an hour. He has stopped looking at the rating.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP regrets to inform you that the lander's insurance excludes 'acts of planet'! CHIP has argued with the policy! The policy is very old! It has seen this before!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the lander can be held down if someone holds it. Hands on the anchors, all of them. It's the only plan that keeps everything, so naturally it's the one you'll argue with.

body:
The planet always shows the same face to its star. One side is a desert that has never seen night. The other is a glacier that has never seen day. Between them, in a narrow band of permanent twilight, the air is breathable and the landing team has set down.

Now the wind is changing. The hot side's air has been pouring toward the cold side for a billion years, and something has shifted that flow toward the twilight band. On the horizon, under a sky the colour of a bruise, a wall of dust is coming.

choices.text: Brace the lander and ride it out

perfect.narrative: The front hits like a wall. You call the bracing beat by beat and the lander holds, rocking on its anchors, dust screaming over it for six hours. When it passes, the lander is buried to the hatch and dented and whole. Everyone in it is fine. Everyone in it will tell this story for the rest of their lives.

good.narrative: The lander holds, just. One anchor pulls and the hull takes the storm side-on for an hour before you get it braced again. Twelve points of hull, and a lot of sand in a lot of places.

poor.narrative: Two anchors go. The lander slides sixty metres across the twilight band with the crew inside it, tumbling. It stops against a ridge. Twenty-two points of hull, and someone is hurt badly enough that the rest of the trip will be careful around them.

outcome.narrative: Everyone on the anchors, braced, and the storm hits.

{crew.pilot} lifts off with the front ten minutes out, flying straight up through air already full of grit. The lander shakes all the way to orbit. You leave the survey gear on the ground and most of the fuel in the sky, but everybody is aboard and the dust never catches you.

choices.text: Abandon the lander and run for the ship

outcome.narrative: You leave the lander anchored and bring the crew up on the emergency tether lift, in suits, through the first edge of the storm. Everyone makes it. The lander doesn't: by the time the storm passes it is half a kilometre downwind and in pieces. You salvage what you can from orbit. It isn't much.

choices.text: Seal the lander and wait out the storm

outcome.narrative: You seal everything and wait. The storm doesn't pass in hours. It passes in days, eight of them, with the lander buried in dust and the air recycler running on prayer. When the sky finally clears to its usual bruise, you dig out and lift off on what's left of the air. Nobody talks much on the way up.

science_link.text: A planet that always shows one face to its star is tidally locked. Models suggest strong winds flowing from the hot day side to the frozen night side.
science_link.label: Tidally locked planets
